claim: ICC Act 1887: railroads first federally regulated; rates reasonable and just; rebates, short-haul discrimination banned; 5 commissioners.

edits.old: The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 made railroads the first industry under federal regulation. Farmers on branch lines had faced 1 carrier, rebates for large shippers, and higher rates for short hauls than long ones. The act required 'just and reasonable' rates, banned rebates and short-haul discrimination, and created a 5-member Interstate Commerce Commission. Its own contradictory terms made it only partly effective.
edits.new: The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 made railroads the first industry under federal regulation. Railroads competed for long hauls but not short ones, and large shippers won rebates that small farmers could not. The act required rates to be 'reasonable and just', banned rebates and charging more for a short haul than a long one on the same line, and created a 5-member Interstate Commerce Commission. Its contradictory terms left it not very effective in practice.

note: Statute reads 'reasonable and just', not 'just and reasonable'; page says no short-haul competition (not '1 carrier') and law 'was not very effective', not 'partly effective'.

claim: Census BDS: annual births/deaths, startups/shutdowns, job creation/destruction, 1978-2023, by establishment/firm characteristics.

edits.old: The Census Bureau's Business Dynamics Statistics measure exactly this churn: establishment births and deaths, firm startups and shutdowns, and job creation and destruction, published every year for the United States from 1978 through 2023 and broken out by industry, firm size, and firm age. The net change in employment at a location is what a headline jobs number shows; the gross flows underneath it are far larger.
edits.new: The Census Bureau's Business Dynamics Statistics measure exactly this churn: establishment births and deaths, firm startups and shutdowns, and job creation and destruction, published annually for the United States with data from 1978 through 2023, for the economy overall and by establishment and firm characteristics. A headline jobs report shows only the net change in employment; the gross flows of jobs created and destroyed underneath it are far larger.

note: Landing page says 'establishment and firm characteristics', not a specific industry/size/age list; 'net change in employment at a location' was unclear. Coverage 1978-2023 confirmed.

claim: Greenspan 1997: Berlin Wall division near-controlled experiment; surpluses/shortages; as much as 5-7x energy per output; verdict negative.

edits.old: In a 1997 speech titled 'The Embrace of Free Markets', the Federal Reserve chairman described the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 as a natural experiment between the 2 systems: planned economies, lacking price signals, produced surpluses of goods nobody wanted beside shortages of goods people needed, and used 5 to 7 times as much energy per unit of output as Western economies. His verdict on rigid central planning: unequivocally negative.

Planned economies, lacking price signals, produced surpluses of goods nobody wanted beside shortages of goods people needed, and used as much as 5 to 7 times more energy per unit of output than the West. His verdict on rigid central planning: unequivocally negative.

note: Speech says energy use was 'as much as five to seven times higher' (upper bound, dropped in card) and calls the division, not the Wall's fall, 'as close to a controlled experiment' as possible.

claim: Collectivization 20% planned, ~97% by 1940; ~1M kulak households (~5M people) deported; famine 1932-33.

edits.old: Collectivization replaces individual farms with large state-directed collectives. The economic logic planners gave was scale and control: pooled land and machinery would raise yields, and the state could take the grain surplus to feed cities and pay for industry. The record shows the reverse in the Soviet case. Removing ownership removed the incentive to produce, resistance was met with force, and output collapsed. It is the clearest historical illustration of what happens when property rights in food are abolished.
edits.new: Collectivization replaces individual farms with large state-directed collectives. The economic logic planners gave was scale and control: pooled land and machinery would raise yields, and the state could take the grain surplus to feed cities and pay for industry. The record shows the reverse in the Soviet case. Removing ownership removed the incentive to produce, resistance was met with force, and output collapsed. Historians often cite it as a stark case of what can follow when farmers lose ownership of what they grow.

note: Example figures verified verbatim on LOC page (curl). Definition stated a sweeping superlative as fact; softened and attributed.

claim: Price held below clearing level causes shortage; planned prices fixed by decree so queues ration; St. Louis Fed rent-control example.

edits.old: When a price is held below the level at which supply equals demand, more is wanted than is offered, and the gap is a shortage. In a market that shortage pushes the price up until some buyers drop out and sellers add supply. A planned economy fixes prices by decree, so the adjustment cannot happen through price. It happens instead through waiting: queues, waiting lists, connections, and informal markets at higher prices. Time, not money, becomes the rationing device.
edits.new: A planned economy sets prices by decree and changes them rarely, so when a fixed price sits below the level at which supply equals demand, the resulting shortage cannot close through a price rise as it would in a market. The gap is closed instead by waiting and access: queues, waiting lists, personal connections, and informal markets at higher prices. Time and influence, not money alone, become the rationing devices.

edits.old: The St. Louis Fed's primer on prices describes the mechanism with a rent-control example: at a ceiling below the market rent, the number of apartments renters want exceeds the number landlords supply, and a shortage results. Administered prices in a planned economy are ceilings on nearly everything at once, so the queue for 1 good was matched by queues for dozens of others.
edits.new: The St. Louis Fed's primer on prices describes the mechanism with rent control: at a ceiling below the market rent, the quantity of apartments renters demand exceeds the quantity landlords supply, and a shortage results. Where a planner holds many prices below that level at once, the same gap opens in 1 market after another, so queues become a routine part of shopping rather than an exception.

note: Definition largely repeated core sd-006 and mkt-008 (ceiling means shortage/queues); refocused on planning. 'Ceilings on nearly everything' overstated and not sourced. Rent-control passage verified.

claim: WWII US rationed gasoline, rubber, sugar, butter, meat; 1943 posters; WPB chairman quote.

edits.old: During the Second World War the United States rationed gasoline, rubber, sugar, butter, and meat. National Archives posters from 1943 urged civilians to share rides and to save waste fats for explosives, explaining that shortages existed because the goods were going to the troops. The War Production Board's chairman put the priority bluntly: the military would get 'astronomical quantities of everything.'
edits.new: During the Second World War the United States rationed gasoline, rubber, sugar, butter, and meat. National Archives posters from 1943 urged civilians to share rides and to save waste fats for explosives, explaining that shortages existed because the goods were going to the troops. The War Production Board's chairman described the military's view of wartime industry as a demand for 'astronomical quantities of everything', with little regard for civilian needs.

note: Nelson was describing the military's view ('...and to hell with civilian needs'), not stating the priority himself. Card misattributed the stance. Other facts verified.
